title: Functions and parameter passing
intro: Review how arguments reach a function, then compare reference and pointer parameters.
question: What values remain in x and y after each swap call?
answer: After swapValue: 5 and 10. After swapReference: 10 and 5. The first function changes copies; the second changes the caller’s variables.

exercise.task: Write increment(int&) to add 1 to its argument. Call it twice on x initially equal to 5.
exercise.hint: Use a non-const reference and increment the parameter itself.
exercise.explanation: The output is 7. Replacing int& with int changes a local copy and leaves x at 5.

title: Recursion
intro: Identify the base case and the progress made by each recursive call.
question: Why does printN(5) print ascending numbers even though n decreases?
answer: The recursive call happens before printing. On the way back from the base case, the calls print 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

exercise.task: Write recursive factorial for n >= 0. Test 0, 1, and 5. Use small inputs to avoid overflow.
exercise.hint: Return 1 when n is 0 or 1; otherwise multiply n by factorial(n-1).
exercise.explanation: The output is 1 1 120. The precondition is n >= 0. A fixed-width integer cannot represent arbitrarily large factorials.

title: Pointers and references
intro: Distinguish an address, a pointed-to value, and an alias.
question: After int& num = x; num = y;, does num refer to y?
answer: No. It still refers to x. The assignment copies y’s value into x.

exercise.task: Use two pointers to x. Modify x through one and print it through the other. Then reseat only the first pointer to y.
exercise.hint: Copying an address makes pointers refer to the same object; reseating one pointer does not reseat the other.
exercise.explanation: The output is 20 followed by 10 20. b keeps the address of x.

title: Const and pointers
intro: Read each declaration by asking whether the data, the pointer, or both are protected.
question: Can const int* p point to a non-const int? Can *p modify it?
answer: Yes, p can point to a non-const int. No, writing through p is prohibited. The original variable can still be modified through another non-const access path.

exercise.task: Add a const pointer to const data. Print its value; document the two assignments the compiler would reject.
exercise.hint: Use const int* const. Keep intentional errors commented out.
exercise.explanation: The pointer cannot be reseated and cannot be used to write the pointed-to value. x itself remains mutable.

title: Scope and static locals
intro: Compare name lookup with storage duration.
question: Why do repeated calls to foo print 1 1, then 1 2, then 1 3?
answer: The ordinary local x is initialized to 1 on each call. The static local y is initialized once and retains the increments.

exercise.task: Write nextId() using a static local counter. Three calls should return 1, 2, and 3.
exercise.hint: Return the counter after incrementing it.
exercise.explanation: The static local persists across calls but its name is visible only inside nextId.

title: One-dimensional arrays
intro: Work with array bounds and compare iteration with recursion.
question: What is the sum of int a[5] = {1,2,5};?
answer: 8. The last two elements are initialized to zero. The original document’s {1,2,3} comments were inconsistent with the initializer.

exercise.task: Write a recursive function that counts even elements. Test {1,2,5,0,0}.
exercise.hint: The empty prefix has zero even elements. Add 1 when the last element is even.
exercise.explanation: The output is 3. Zero is even. Never access a[n] when n is the number of elements.

title: Console input and output
intro: Read complete lines, validate numeric input, and format results.
question: What is the difference between cin >> name and getline(cin, name)?
answer: >> reads one whitespace-delimited word. getline reads up to the newline and can retain spaces inside a full name.
lesson:
Streams carry data

Include <iostream> for std::cin, std::cout, and std::cerr. The operator << inserts data into an output stream; >> extracts and converts input. Chain operations to read or print several values.

std::getline(cin, name) reads a full line. After numeric extraction, a newline may remain in the stream; the second example shows how to discard that line before using getline.

Always check extraction before using input. A failed conversion sets a stream error state. An interactive retry loop would call cin.clear() and discard the invalid line before trying again. These small programs report an error and stop instead.

<iomanip> supplies fixed and setprecision. With fixed, precision means the number of digits after the decimal point. In this page, enter all input in the input box before Run; prompts do not open an interactive terminal.

exercise.task: Read two grades in [0,100]. Print their average with one digit after the decimal point. Reject nonnumeric or out-of-range input.
exercise.hint: Use double values, test both extractions, then apply fixed and setprecision(1).
exercise.explanation: With input 80 91, the output is Average: 85.5. Integer division is avoided by using double.

title: Reading and writing text files
intro: Use file streams and check that opening, writing, and reading succeed.
question: Why is while (!in.eof()) a poor way to read records?
answer: eof() describes a previous operation; it does not predict the next read. Test the extraction itself so you do not process stale data after a failed read.
lesson:
A file stream has an open/close lifetime

Include <fstream>. Use ofstream to write, ifstream to read, or fstream for both. Once open, a file stream uses the same <<, >>, and getline operations as console streams.

The relative path grades.txt is resolved from the program’s working directory, which may differ from the directory containing its source. Check if (!stream) after opening. Close the writer before reading so buffered data is flushed. A stream also closes automatically when its object goes out of scope.

Normal ofstream opening truncates an existing file. Add ios::app to append instead. The record format below permits single-word names; use a line-based format or a delimiter if names can contain spaces.

Online files are temporary. This example writes and reads its own file in one run. It does not access files on your computer, and a later Run starts a separate sandbox. Download the program to keep its generated file locally: g++ -std=c++17 example.cpp -o example, then ./example. If the online service blocks file access, use that local workflow.

exercise.task: After writing Amal 85 and Lina 92, append Omar 78 using ios::app. Read all three records and print their average.
exercise.hint: Close the first output stream, open a second one with ios::app, close it, then open the input stream.
exercise.explanation: The names and grades are printed, followed by Average: 85.0. Opening with ios::app preserves the existing records.

title: Classes and Objects
intro: Learn to model state and behavior, construct independent objects, and protect their data through a clear interface.
question: Which quadrant contains (-3,0), and what is its distance to (4,0)?
answer: It lies on an axis, so whichQuadrant returns -1. Its distance to (4,0) is 7.

exercise.task: Add a const distanceToOrigin() member. Test points (3,4) and (0,0).
exercise.hint: You can reuse distanceMember with a default-constructed Point.
exercise.explanation: The output is 5 0. The const qualifier allows this query on a const Point.

title: Copy construction and destruction
intro: Trace object lifetimes without relying on compiler-dependent return-value copies.
question: Which call copies p1: byValue(p1) or byReference(p1)?
answer: byValue(p1) copies this lvalue. byReference(p1) binds a reference and does not construct a separate Point.

exercise.task: Create one outer Point and one inner Point in a nested scope. Predict the destructor order.
exercise.hint: The inner object is destroyed at the closing brace of its scope.
exercise.explanation: The inner Point is destroyed before the message. The outer Point is destroyed at the end of main.
exercise.output:
Construct (1,1)
Construct (2,2)
Destroy (2,2)
Back in outer scope
Destroy (1,1)

title: Interface and implementation
intro: Separate declarations from definitions while preserving the same behavior.
question: Why should point.h use an include guard?
answer: It prevents repeated definitions when the same header is included more than once in a translation unit. Separate .cpp files still need to be compiled and linked.

exercise.task: Add getX() const: put its declaration in the interface section and definition in the implementation section. Print the x coordinate.
exercise.hint: The definition outside the class uses Point::getX.
exercise.explanation: The output is 3. In the real multi-file project, add the declaration to point.h and definition to point.cpp.

title: Arrays of objects
intro: Construct every array element and process objects through const interfaces.
question: If two Points have the same distance to the origin, which does closestToOrigin choose?
answer: It chooses the first one because it replaces best only for a strictly smaller distance.

exercise.task: Change closestToOrigin to select the last Point on a tie. Test {(3,4),(0,5),(1,0),(-1,0)}.
exercise.hint: Replace the strict comparison with <=.
exercise.explanation: The output is (-1,0). The function’s nonempty-array precondition remains necessary.

title: Const members and temperature conversion
intro: Separate immutable units from mutable readings; distinguish values from differences.
question: Starting at 0°C, what is the result of an increase of 18°F?
answer: 10°C, equivalent to 50°F. For a temperature difference use 18 × 5/9; subtracting 32 would convert an absolute reading instead.

exercise.task: Create 0°C and 32°F objects. Increase the first by 18°F and the second by 10°C. Print both and their average in Celsius.
exercise.hint: Use changeT to convert differences, and tempAvgArray to convert absolute readings.
exercise.explanation: Both objects represent 10°C (50°F); the average is 10°C.

title: Const and static class members
intro: Distinguish object-specific state from shared class state.
question: Can a const member function modify a static member?
answer: Yes. A const member function protects the non-mutable instance state through this; a static member is not part of that instance.

exercise.task: Print the live Box count before, inside, and after a nested scope containing two Boxes.
exercise.hint: Use Box::getCount(). A copied Box also counts as a new live object.
exercise.explanation: The output is 0, 2, 0. Destruction restores the count when the scope ends.

title: Composition
intro: Model a “has-a” relationship using member objects.
question: If the original Point a changes after constructing Line(a,b), does the Line change?
answer: No. This Line stores independent Point values initialized by copying the endpoints.

exercise.task: Construct a Line from (0,0) to (3,4), change the original endpoint b to (6,8), and print the Line length again.
exercise.hint: Line stores values, not references to the original endpoints.
exercise.explanation: The output remains 5. Storing references instead would change both lifetime requirements and behavior.

title: Dynamic memory
intro: Trace allocation, ownership, and deallocation as separate steps.
question: Why is delete[] required for an allocation made with new Point[5]?
answer: It matches array allocation and destroys each element. Mixing new[] with delete is undefined behavior.

exercise.task: Allocate an array of three Points, initialize them to (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), print them, and release the array.
exercise.hint: Use new Point[3] with an initializer list and delete[].
exercise.explanation: All three Points are printed, and array storage is released exactly once. No pointer is used after deletion.

title: Dynamic memory inside a class
intro: An owning class must define what copying and destruction mean.
question: What goes wrong if two Students shallow-copy the same owning grades pointer?
answer: They share one allocation unintentionally. Destroying both can double-delete it, and changes through one affect the other. Deep copies give each Student independent storage.

exercise.task: Test self-assignment (a=a), copy assignment (b=a), and independent modification of b.
exercise.hint: The this != &other guard handles self-assignment. Copy assignment must allocate a separate array.
exercise.explanation: With input 70 80 90, a stays unchanged and b starts with 75. Their averages are 80 and approximately 81.6667.

title: Friend functions and classes
intro: Grant access deliberately and compare broad with narrow friendship.
question: If B is a friend of A, is A automatically a friend of B?
answer: No. Friendship is not reciprocal. It is also not transitive or inherited.

exercise.task: Change the friend function of ClassA and ClassB to return their product instead of their sum.
exercise.hint: Update the declaration in both classes, the definition, and the call consistently.
exercise.explanation: The output is 83300. Both classes must authorize the same function signature.

title: The this pointer and returned objects
intro: Ask whether a function result is a new value or an alias to an existing object.
question: What does a.byValue().boo() change, and what does a.byReference().boo() change?
answer: The first changes a temporary copy. The second changes a itself. The displayed values are 5 then 60.

exercise.task: Add add(int) returning A& and use a.add(10).add(20). Starting from 5, print the final value.
exercise.hint: Modify x and return *this by reference to enable chaining.
exercise.explanation: The output is 35. Returning a value would make later chained changes affect a temporary.

title: Inheritance
intro: Use public inheritance for an “is-a” relationship and trace the base subobject.
question: Why can UnderGrad call Student::print but cannot directly read Student’s private ID?
answer: The public function is accessible through public inheritance. ID remains private to Student, even though it exists inside the base subobject.

exercise.task: Add a graduationYear member to UnderGrad, initialize it through its constructor, and print it after the training company.
exercise.hint: Add a constructor argument, a member, an initialization, and an output statement.
exercise.explanation: The output includes 2027. The base constructor still runs first and the derived destructor still runs first.
exercise.output:
Base const.
Derived const.
123 Leila Ali
ABC
2027
Derived DEST
Base DEST

title: Polymorphism and abstract classes
intro: Use a shared interface while preserving object-specific behavior.
question: Why does Animal* pointing to a Cat print Meow when makeSound is called?
answer: makeSound is virtual. The final overrider for the actual Cat object runs, rather than choosing solely from the pointer’s static type.

exercise.task: Add a Cow subclass implementing makeSound. Call it through Animal*.
exercise.hint: The override must match the base signature. The subclass becomes concrete when all inherited pure virtual functions are implemented.
exercise.explanation: The output includes Moo. The pointer is non-owning and must not be deleted because cow is a local object.

title: Upcasting and checked downcasting
intro: Use checked casts when a derived-specific operation is required.
question: What is the difference between failed pointer and reference dynamic_cast?
answer: A failed pointer cast returns nullptr. A failed reference cast throws std::bad_cast. Downcasting requires a polymorphic base for these runtime checks.

exercise.task: Make shape_ptr point to a Circle instead of a Rectangle. Predict which cast succeeds.
exercise.hint: Only the Circle cast should succeed.
exercise.explanation: The Rectangle cast fails, and the Circle cast draws a circle. The virtual base destructor permits safe deletion.
exercise.output:
Could not cast shape_ptr to a Rectangle
Drawing a circle

title: Multiple and multilevel inheritance
intro: Distinguish a chain of inheritance from a class with more than one direct base.
question: Which relationship is multilevel, and which is multiple?
answer: ResearchStudent → Student → Person is multilevel. ResearchStudent’s direct bases Student and Presenter demonstrate multiple inheritance.

exercise.task: Add teach() to Presenter and invoke it on ResearchStudent.
exercise.hint: The inherited public function is accessible on the derived object.
exercise.explanation: The additional output is Teaching a tutorial. If both bases supplied the same member name, explicit qualification could resolve ambiguity.
exercise.output:
Name: Leila
Studying C++
Presenting research
Teaching a tutorial

title: Operator overloading
intro: Preserve familiar operator semantics and return types.
question: Why return bool from == and a reference from assignment or +=?
answer: Equality expresses a true/false result. Returning a reference to the updated left operand lets assignment and compound assignment participate in chaining.

exercise.task: Add unary + to Point as a const member that returns an unchanged copy. Verify that +p compares equal to p.
exercise.hint: The implementation can simply return *this by value.
exercise.explanation: The output is true. Unary + returns a value without modifying p.

title: Prefix/postfix and stream input
intro: Compare the value of an expression with the state after evaluating it.
question: Starting at 65, what values do s++ and then ++s display?
answer: s++ displays the old grade, 65, while changing it to 66. ++s then changes it to 67 and displays 67.

exercise.task: Add prefix and postfix decrement with the same return conventions as increment. Test s-- followed by --s.
exercise.hint: Prefix returns *this by reference. Postfix saves a copy before changing the object.
exercise.explanation: The grades displayed are 65, 64, and 63. The postfix int parameter is a signature marker, not the amount to subtract.
